title: How I Use AI to Protect My Mental Health Without Losing My Creativity
summary: AI changed how I create, and how I feel. Here's how I set AI and mental health boundaries to protect my confidence, ease anxiety, and keep my creative voice.
body_markdown:
## My Creative Life Before AI


Before AI entered the picture, creativity was something I had a very specific relationship with. It wasn’t just a skill; it was part of how I understood myself. I’ve always worked in roles that center writing and storytelling: marketing, content strategy, podcasting, freelance writing. Creativity wasn’t something I did occasionally; it was something I relied on. And for the most part, I took pride in being able to generate ideas from scratch, even when it was hard.


But then “productivity” entered. I felt pressure to work faster, generate more ideas for social media, more blog posts, create double the amount of content than I was typically producing. To no one’s surprise, the more content I “created,” the actual “creativity” went away. Looking back, that was my first real taste of creative burnout – long before AI was ever part of the equation.


There were creative blocks that lasted longer than I wanted to admit. Blank pages that felt more intimidating than they should have. Overthinking that turned simple ideas into complicated ones. And a constant undercurrent of[self-doubt](https://lifestance.com/blog/overcoming-intrusive-negative-thoughts-self-doubt/) , questioning whether anything I made was actually good enough.


Creativity wasn’t always flowing or joyful. Sometimes it felt slow, messy, and frustrating. But there was also something meaningful about it. Wrestling with an idea until it finally made sense felt like part of the process of making it mine.


But then AI entered the picture. When I first started using AI tools, it was mostly out of curiosity. I wanted to see what they could do. Could they save me time by writing the social media captions that I didn’t want to write? Could it help me brainstorm story ideas based on SEO? Yes, and more. It immediately became useful in ways I couldn’t anticipate. And in turn, it became part of my workflow.


At first, there was also something relieving about it, less time stuck in uncertainty, more time actually building something. Some projects that would have previously taken hours just to get started suddenly had momentum in minutes.


But alongside that ease came a subtle shift I didn’t fully notice at first. Because the easier something becomes, the more invisible the process can feel.
